title: Designating an Angels Advocate
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece introduces a counterpart to the familiar Devil's Advocate: an Angel's Advocate who argues the upside case for a decision rather than defending it uncritically. The author notes that teams caught up in momentum rarely need someone to point out opportunity, but a designated skeptic paired with a designated optimist produces a more balanced discussion than either role alone. Timing matters -- both advocates should enter only once a proposal is well developed, not before the team has had a chance to understand it on its own terms. The piece is aimed at leaders designing better decision processes, especially for risk-averse teams or those still recovering from a recent setback.
points: A Devil's Advocate surfaces risk; an Angel's Advocate surfaces the possibilities of a successful outcome.
Neither role should be introduced until a proposal has already been well explored by the team.
Using both advocates together produces a more robust, less lopsided discussion than either alone.
Risk-averse teams or those recovering from a recent setback benefit most from an Angel's Advocate.
quotes: Hearing all of the viewpoints, positive and negative, allows the team to make the best decision possible.
Leaders understand the power of the Devil’s Advocate , someone who plays the role of chief doubter and critic in the discussion of an important decision.
The Advocate plays an important role by pointing out the downside, potential risks, and likely problems associated with a decision or strategy.
Leaders sometimes designate a team member to play this role, although there is usually one colleague who does so without being asked.

Given that leaders and teams often get behind an idea, decision, or strategy with a big momentum forward, and without questioning the downside, it seems unlikely that someone who points out the upside and opportunity at hand would add much value.
Just like a Devil’s Advocate is not just a critic or skeptic, an Angel’s Advocate doesn’t just focus on the positive or cheer the team on.
Instead, an Angel’s Advocate asks the “What If?” question and points out the possibilities if the decision and strategy were successful.
Such an Advocate focuses most on what would change as a result of a successful outcome, highlighting the many benefits that are hard to visualize during the decision process.
